opus-5.5.text:
Pairing is one of the things I'd point to if someone asked what's distinctive about how we work. The most obvious benefit is knowledge transfer. When you sit with someone for a few hours on a real problem, you pick up things you'd never get from reading their code or a design doc: how they debug, which tools they reach for, what they check first when a training run looks off, which shortcuts they trust and which they don't. A lot of the most valuable engineering knowledge is tacit like that. It doesn't get written down, it just lives in people's habits.

It's also really good for onboarding. Someone new can be productive in a codebase much faster if they pair with someone who knows it, instead of spending weeks reading and asking questions. And it goes both ways. The person who's been around a while often learns something from the newcomer, because they bring fresh eyes and question things everyone else takes for granted.

There's a focus benefit too. When you're pairing, you don't drift off to check Slack or go down a rabbit hole for an hour. Having someone next to you keeps you honest. You talk through your reasoning out loud, and half the time just explaining what you're about to do makes you realize it's the wrong approach.

And for the kind of work we do, where a subtle bug in a large training run can cost a lot of compute and time, having two people thinking about the code as it's written catches mistakes earlier. It isn't a replacement for review, but it shifts some of that scrutiny to the moment you're making decisions, which is when it's cheapest to fix things.

The last thing I'd mention is cultural. Pairing helps build a sense that the work is shared. It's less "this is my code, that's yours" and more that we're all trying to get the same thing right. I think that matters a lot at a place where the stakes feel high and you want people comfortable saying, "Wait, I'm not sure this is right."

r001.rationale: The response describes shared ownership and working toward the same goal, but does not frame asking for help as imposing on someone versus collaborating on a shared project.

r002.rationale: It says pairing reveals tacit habits that code or design docs would not show, but does not explain that asking for advice would typically leave those habits unspoken.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so one thing I'd say about Anthropic is that we actually do a lot of pair programming, and I think it's one of my favourite things about how we work. The basic idea is just two people sitting at one computer, one of them typing and the other one watching, talking through what's happening. And I think a lot of people hear that and assume it's a 2x cost — you've got two engineers producing one person's worth of output. But that's really not been my experience.

There are a few things I value about it. The first is just that it's a really fast way to learn. When I joined Anthropic, pairing with people who already knew the codebase was by far the fastest way to get up to speed. You see how someone else actually navigates the code, what shortcuts they use, how they debug when something goes wrong — all this tacit knowledge that would never make it into documentation. And it goes the other way too: when someone new joins and pairs with me, I'm constantly picking up things from them.

The second is that it's a forcing function for clarity. If I'm about to go write something and I have to explain to the person next to me what I'm about to do and why, I often realise halfway through the explanation that the plan doesn't quite make sense, or there's a simpler approach. You catch a lot of mistakes before they happen rather than after.

The third thing — and I think this is underrated — is that it's just more fun and more energising. Engineering can be pretty isolating. You can spend a whole day staring at a stack trace by yourself. Having someone there to talk it through with keeps you engaged, keeps you from going down rabbit holes for hours, and it builds relationships across the team. People who've paired a lot end up with a shared understanding of the systems and of each other, which makes everything else — code review, design discussions, incident response — go more smoothly.

I'd also say it fits the kind of work we do pretty well. A lot of training infrastructure is fiddly and high-stakes — if you get something subtly wrong in a distributed training run, it might not show up for days and it can be very expensive. Having a second set of eyes on that in real time is genuinely valuable, in a way it might not be for every kind of software.

So I don't think it's right for 100% of tasks. There's plenty of work where you just need to go heads-down on your own. But as a default mode for a lot of what we do, I think it's been a big part of why the team works well together.

r001.rationale: The response describes two people working together, but does not frame pairing as turning a request for help into collaboration on a shared project.

r002.rationale: It says pairing reveals tacit knowledge about navigating code and debugging, but does not explain that asking for advice would typically leave those habits unspoken.

astra-6.text:
What I really value is how much you learn from working closely with someone else. When you’re pair programming, you don’t just see the code they produce — you see how they approach a problem, what questions they ask, and when they decide to step back and try something different. A lot of that is hard to communicate in a code review.

And it makes asking for help feel very natural. If you’re stuck, you can bring someone in and work through it together. I think that’s particularly valuable when you’re joining a team: you get productive faster, but you also build relationships and get comfortable thinking out loud with people.

r001.rationale: It says asking for help feels natural and that people can work through a problem together, but does not frame help-seeking as moving from imposing on someone to collaborating on a shared project.

r002.rationale: It describes seeing a colleague’s approach and questions, but says these are hard to communicate in code review; it does not explain that asking for advice would leave those working habits unspoken.

sol-6.1.text:
What I value most is how much context gets shared. When you’re working closely with someone on a real problem, you learn how they think, why the code is structured the way it is, and which approaches they’ve already tried. A lot of that is hard to capture in documentation.

It also makes it easier to ask questions early. If you’re working alone, you can spend a long time stuck on something because you don’t want to interrupt anyone. When you’re pairing, asking questions is just part of the work. And both people can learn from it, even when one has much more experience with that particular part of the system.

r001.rationale: It contrasts hesitating to ask for help because it might interrupt someone with pairing, where questions are simply part of working together on a real problem.

r002.rationale: It says pairing reveals how someone thinks, structures code, and which approaches they tried, but does not clearly identify low-level working habits that advice-seeking would leave unspoken.
